did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ezekiel gives an exact date for the prophecy: the ninth year, the tenth month, and the tenth day of the month.
Did you know? On the very day Ezekiel was commanded to write down the date, the king of Babylon began the siege of Jerusalem.
Did you know? Jerusalem is compared to a cooking pot, and the pieces placed in it symbolize the city’s people and its condition under siege.
Did you know? The command is to choose the best sheep, build up a strong fire, and cook the meat until even the bones are charred.
Did you know? Jerusalem is called the “city of bloodshed” and “a pot whose scum is still in it,” because its filth has not been removed; therefore, its pieces are taken out indiscriminately.
Did you know? According to the prophecy, Jerusalem’s blood was poured out on bare rock and was not covered with earth, so it remained exposed and cried out for justice.
Did you know? The pot is placed empty on the coals so that the heat will scorch the bronze and melt away its impurity and scum.
Did you know? Ezekiel is told that his wife, called “the delight of your eyes,” is about to die, and he is commanded not to observe the usual mourning customs.
Did you know? Ezekiel told the people the word of the Lord in the morning, his wife died that evening, and the next morning he did exactly as he had been commanded.
Did you know? When the survivor arrives and reports the destruction, Ezekiel’s mouth will be opened and he will no longer be silent; thus, the prophet will become a sign to the people.
